catalog_quote: Lhokpu語には高調（high tone）と低調（low tone）の音韻論的対立が認められる。またcontour toneとして高昇調（rising tone）が観察される。また高調の異声調（allotone）として、形態素境界では下降調（falling tone）が現れる（[55] → [53] or [54] /____#）。ストレスや発声様式（phonation type）といった超分節音素はこの言語では弁別的ではない。音声レベルでは促声調にも高昇調が存在する。... 複音節語は第一音節が高調の場合は後の音節は低調に、第一音節が低調の場合は第二音節が高調になり第三音節は低調になる。

new_statements.quote: Lhokpu語には高調（high tone）と低調（low tone）の音韻論的対立が認められる。またcontour toneとして高昇調（rising tone）が観察される。また高調の異声調（allotone）として、形態素境界では下降調（falling tone）が現れる（[55] → [53] or [54] /____#）。ストレスや発声様式（phonation type）といった超分節音素はこの言語では弁別的ではない。音声レベルでは促声調にも高昇調が存在する。[…] 複音節語は第一音節が高調の場合は後の音節は低調に、第一音節が低調の場合は第二音節が高調になり第三音節は低調になる。
new_statements.translation: In Lhokpu a phonological opposition between a high tone and a low tone is recognised. In addition, a high-rising tone is observed as a contour tone. Further, as an allotone of the high tone, a falling tone appears at morpheme boundaries ([55] → [53] or [54] /___#). Suprasegmental features such as stress and phonation type are not distinctive in this language. At the phonetic level a high-rising tone also occurs on checked syllables. [...] In polysyllabic words, when the first syllable is high-toned the following syllables are low-toned; when the first syllable is low-toned the second syllable becomes high-toned and the third syllable low-toned.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nishida analyses Lhokpu as having a lexical high/low tone contrast (syllable template (C1)(C2)V(C3)/T) and states explicitly that stress is not distinctive; word-level pitch is fixed by the tone of the first syllable (H-L-L or L-H-L across polysyllables), i.e. one high-pitched syllable per word, located on syllable 1 or 2 depending on lexical tone. No statement of a stress position as such.
new_statements.exceptions: Falling allotone of high tone before a morpheme boundary; phonetic rising tone on checked syllables. Author calls the whole sketch a preliminary essay (試論) based on c. 1,500 words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (polysyllabic word tone patterns); based on elicited basic vocabulary from one consultant (Dawa, b. 1969, native of Taba village), fieldwork in Phuntsholing, Chukha, Dec 2013–Sep 2017.
new_statements.identity_note: Nishida's data are Lhokpu as spoken by one consultant born in Taba village (Samtse; autonym Doyap/Lhokpu), recorded in Phuntsholing 2013–2017 — same language as lhok1238, no separate dialect code. Caveat: Nishida classifies Lhokpu under Tibetic and posits a Dzongkha-like inventory (y, ø, retroflexes, vowel length, nasal vowels, two tones), which conflicts with van Driem (2001) and Grollmann & Gerber (2018), who treat Lhokpu as a non-Tibetic branch (Wikipedia's inventory, presumably from the Bern fieldwork, shows breathy-voiced stops and /ɒ/ instead); the consultant is trilingual in Dzongkha, so heavy contact influence or elicitation artefacts are possible. Treat the 'tone, no distinctive stress' reading as provisional until van Driem 2026 or Grollmann & Gerber 2018 is read.

new_statements.quote: Initial voiceless nasals in Lhokpu are probably a consequence of high tone on the respective syllable and therefore secondary, like the overall tone system of Lhokpu, which looks suspiciously like the Dzongkha system (cf. van Driem 1998: 55–57) and may be a recent, contact-based innovation. However, for the initial voiceless nasals (and other sonorants) of Lhokpu, it is not entirely clear yet whether they are conditioned by high tone or whether they are in fact primary and themselves condition high tone.
new_statements.citation: Grollmann, Selin & Pascal Gerber. 2018. Linguistic evidence for a closer relationship between Lhokpu and Dhimal: Including some remarks on the Dhimalish subgroup. Cahiers de Linguistique Asie Orientale 47(1): 1–96.

The quoted passage is at line ~1644 ff., sec. 4.2.2 'Nasal correspondences' (TOC: p. 30; passage straddles draft pp. 31-32), verbatim; the only interruptions are footnote 21 and the page number '31' falling inside the sentence, plus line-end hyphenation ('re-cent', 'son-orants'). Read the surrounding section: it is about Lhokpu/Dhimal nasal correspondences; the tone remark is incidental (voiceless initial nasals probably secondary to high tone; tone system Dzongkha-like, possibly contact-induced; coda voiceless nasals…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Nishida 2019 statement (high/low tone contrast; stress not distinctive): confirms Lhokpu is tonal and adds that the system looks Dzongkha-like and correlates with voiceless-sonorant initials; silent on stress itself, so it neither confirms nor disputes Nishida's 'stress is not distinctive'. The catalog record (world-2026-09-17) has an empty rule, so nothing to contradict. NOTE on access: the listed open_url (BORIS 145604 'AS-PUBLISHED' PDF) is not open -- the Internet Archive copy of the BORIS record page (2024-09-05) marks the file 'Restricted to registered users only', the archived PDF URL is a 302 to Shibboleth login, and the live boris-portal host served 0 b…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhokpu has a tone system (high tone associated with voiceless-sonorant onsets), described as resembling the Dzongkha register system and possibly a recent contact-induced innovation; the work is a comparative-historical paper and makes no statement about word stress or accent placement. Appendix C.1 lists only segmental consonant and vowel inventories (no prosodic row).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only prosodic hedging is whether voiceless sonorants are conditioned by high tone or themselves condition it. The two occurrences of the word 'stress' in the text are non-prosodic ('needs to be stressed', 'puts too much stress on a single language').
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern the same language, Lhokpu (Lhop/Doya) of southwestern Bhutan, from the 2015 Bern fieldwork; no dialect split is described. Work 0 was read in its 2017 pre-publication draft (academia.edu 32861274 via the Internet Archive), not the Brill-paginated published version.

tone.says: From the Crossref abstract only: presents 'morphological, lexical, and phonological evidence' for Lhokpu-Dhimal and re-examines Dhimalish (Dhimal + Toto). Whether Toto tone or its correspondences are discussed could not be verified (full text walled); listed as a low-confidence comparative-phonology lead that treats this language, not as a confirmed tone work.

sources.note: In the areal phonology overview the authors state that contour tones are attested in Lhokpu (alongside Dzongkha, Chocha-ngacakha, Kurtöp) and that the emergence of tone in Lhokpu in general seems to result from contact with Dzongkha. One sentence; no inventory or number of tones given. Consistent with the statement listed here (Nishida 2019: H/L contrast plus rising contour; Grollmann & Gerber 2018: tone system 'suspiciously like Dzongkha', possibly contact-induced).
